title: Expected Utility
equation: E[u(a, theta)] = sum_theta p(theta) u(a, theta)
everyday_setup: A player chooses before knowing which state of the world is true. Instead of pretending one state is certain, the model weighs each possible payoff by how likely that state seems.
derivation_steps: List the possible hidden states, such as low value and high value.
Attach a probability to each state. These probabilities must add up to one.
Compute the payoff from the action in each state.
Multiply each payoff by its probability and add the pieces.
symbol_by_symbol: a is the action being evaluated. theta is the unknown state or type. p(theta) is the probability of that state. u(a, theta) is the payoff if action a is chosen and theta is true. The summation adds the probability-weighted payoffs.
why_it_matters: This is the bridge from uncertainty to choice. Bayesian games, auctions, and screening problems all need a way to compare actions before hidden information is revealed.
common_misread: The formula is not saying the average state actually happens. It is a decision rule for choosing under uncertainty.

title: Best Response
everyday_setup: A move is not good by itself. It is good against some belief or opponent action. Best response asks what player i should do after holding the rest of the situation fixed.
derivation_steps: Fix what the other players are doing.
Try each available action for player i.
Compute player i's payoff for each candidate action.
Keep the action or actions with the highest payoff.
symbol_by_symbol: BR_i is player i's best-response set. a_-i means the actions of everyone except player i. argmax means the action that makes the payoff as large as possible. u_i is player i's payoff function.
why_it_matters: Best response is the local engine behind Nash equilibrium, rationalizability, mixed strategies, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, and many deviation checks.
common_misread: A best response is always conditional. If the opponent action or belief changes, the best response may change too.

title: Nash Equilibrium
equation: a_i in BR_i(a_-i) for every player i
everyday_setup: A proposed prediction must survive every player asking whether they alone would rather switch. Nash equilibrium is the point where all those one-person checks pass at once.
derivation_steps: Start with a proposed action profile.
For each player, hold the other players' actions fixed.
Check whether the player's assigned action is a best response.
If every player passes the check, the profile is a Nash equilibrium.
symbol_by_symbol: a_i is player i's chosen action. a_-i is everyone else's action. BR_i(a_-i) is the set of best responses against those other actions. The phrase for every player means no one is exempt from the deviation check.
why_it_matters: It turns strategic prediction into a mutual consistency test. The result can be stable even when it is inefficient, unfair, or socially bad.
common_misread: Equilibrium does not mean the best overall outcome. It means no single player wants to move alone under the modeled payoffs.

title: Backward Induction
everyday_setup: A threat or promise matters only if it will still be attractive later. Backward induction solves later choices first and uses them to interpret earlier choices.
derivation_steps: Go to the final decision points in the game tree.
At each final decision, choose the branch with the best payoff for the player moving there.
Replace that decision point with the value of the chosen continuation.
Move one step earlier and repeat until the start of the tree is reached.
symbol_by_symbol: V(node) is the value of arriving at a decision point. max_action means choose the action with the highest continuation value. next node is the future decision point or outcome reached by that action.
why_it_matters: It separates credible future behavior from empty threats. Dynamic games, bargaining, finite repetition, and subgame perfection all depend on this recursive logic.
common_misread: Solving backward is only as good as the tree. If the tree leaves out information, renegotiation, or hidden types, the backward calculation can be precise but misleading.

title: Discounted Payoff Sum
equation: U = u_0 + delta u_1 + delta^2 u_2 + ...
everyday_setup: Repeated interaction asks whether future consequences can discipline today's temptation. The discount factor says how strongly the future counts today.
derivation_steps: Write the payoff from the current period.
Write the payoff from each future period.
Multiply each future payoff by an extra power of delta for each step into the future.
Add current and discounted future payoffs into one present-value comparison.
symbol_by_symbol: U is total discounted payoff. u_0 is payoff now. u_1 is next period's payoff. delta is between zero and one and measures patience. delta squared means a payoff two periods away receives two rounds of discounting.
why_it_matters: Cooperation, cartel discipline, and bargaining delay all depend on whether discounted future gains or losses outweigh current temptation.
common_misread: The formula does not make future punishment automatically powerful. If delta is small, future consequences may barely matter.

title: Bayes Rule
equation: P(type | signal) = P(signal | type) P(type) / P(signal)
everyday_setup: After observing an action or signal, a player revises what they believe about hidden type. Bayes rule is the bookkeeping that turns prior belief plus observed evidence into posterior belief.
derivation_steps: Start with the prior probability of the type.
Ask how likely the observed signal would be if that type were true.
Multiply prior probability by signal likelihood.
Normalize by the total probability of seeing that signal across all possible types.
symbol_by_symbol: P(type | signal) is the updated belief after seeing the signal. P(signal | type) is how likely that signal is for that type. P(type) is the prior belief. P(signal) rescales all type weights so the updated probabilities add to one.
why_it_matters: PBE, signaling, screening, and Bayesian games need beliefs that respond to observations rather than floating freely.
common_misread: Bayes rule does not tell you off-path beliefs when the observed signal has zero probability under the proposed strategy. That is why dynamic information games need careful belief discipline.

title: Auction Expected Payment
equation: expected payment = payment if win x probability of winning
everyday_setup: A bidder does not only ask what they pay if they win. They also ask how likely the bid is to win. The expected payment combines those two pieces.
derivation_steps: Pick a bid.
Find what the bidder would pay if that bid wins under the auction rule.
Find the probability that this bid wins against rival bids.
Multiply the payment-if-win by the probability of winning.
symbol_by_symbol: The payment-if-win comes from the auction format. The probability of winning comes from beliefs about rival bids or values. Their product is the average payment before knowing whether this bid wins.
why_it_matters: Revenue equivalence, bid shading, first-price auctions, and ad auctions all require separating the price paid from the chance of paying it.
common_misread: A higher bid can raise both the chance of winning and the payment made when winning. The bidder's incentive depends on both effects, not one alone.

title: Common Knowledge Recursion
everyday_setup: Coordination can require more than everyone privately knowing the same fact. Players may need to know that others know, and know that others know that others know.
derivation_steps: Start with an event E.
Add the statement that everyone knows E.
Add the statement that everyone knows that everyone knows E.
Continue the chain without stopping at any finite level.
symbol_by_symbol: E is the event. K is the knowledge operator. KE means everyone knows E. KKE means everyone knows that everyone knows E. The dots mean the chain continues indefinitely.
why_it_matters: Public announcements, coordination, rationalizability, and equilibrium reasoning often depend on shared awareness rather than private information alone.
common_misread: A fact being true or widely known is not enough. Common knowledge requires the recursive publicness that lets players reason about other players' reasoning.
